title: Generation Averages
aka: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
story: A lab grows a cell culture from one starting cell. Each cell splits into at most two daughter cells. The lab records the family as a binary tree: every node holds a cell's size in micrometres, and its children are the cells it split into.
To spot whether cells shrink over time, the lab wants the average size of each generation: the starting cell, then its daughters, then theirs, and so on.
task: Write generationAverages(root). Return a list with the average node value of each level of the tree, from the top level down.

An empty tree gives an empty list. Trees are shown in level order, like [12, 8, 10, 7, 9, null, 15], where null marks a missing child. Your function receives real TreeNode objects with val, left and right.
constraints: Answers within 0.000001 of the expected value are accepted.

examples.explanation: Generation 1 is just 12. Generation 2 is 8 and 10, average 9. Generation 3 is 7, 9 and 15 (the null is a missing cell), average 31 / 3 = 10.333…
A single starting cell that never split: one generation, average 5.

hints: Forget averages for a moment. How would you get the list of cells in generation 2? In generation 3?
Each generation is exactly the children of the previous generation. If you have all of generation k in a list, you can build generation k + 1 from it.
Process the tree one level at a time with a queue. The trick is knowing where one level ends and the next begins. What do you know about the queue's length right when a level starts?

Put the root in a queue. While it is not empty: read size = queue.length, pop exactly size nodes, add up their values, push their children, then record sum / size. Those size nodes were exactly one level.
bruteForce: Do a depth-first walk, passing the depth along, and keep a sum and a count per depth in two lists. Then divide.

That is actually O(n) and perfectly fine. It is listed here because it is a natural first idea. The breadth-first version matches the question more directly: "per level" is exactly what BFS gives you, one level at a time.

js: *   this.val = val; this.left = left; this.right = right;
* TreeNode is already defined for you.
* @return {number[]} average of each level, top first
py: # TreeNode is already defined for you.

walkthrough: Breadth-first search visits the tree level by level. The only extra step is to handle one whole level at a time so you can average it.
• Level holds [7, 9, 15]. Sum 31, size 3, average 10.333…. No children, so stop.
The JavaScript version builds a fresh array for each level. The Python version uses one queue and reads its length at the start of each level. Both are the same idea.
solution.timeWhy: Every node is added to the queue once and removed once.
solution.spaceWhy: The queue holds at most one level, where w is the widest level (up to about n / 2).
solution.takeaway: Any question that says "per level" or "per generation" is a breadth-first search question. Snapshot the queue length at the start of a level to know exactly which nodes belong to it.
